text: Can teacher-guided edge removal make GNNs cheaper while preserving node-classification accuracy?
A proposal for sparse graph learning with knowledge distillation

Target: 1 minute(s).

Introduce the problem and frame this as a proposal. State that the completed evidence is currently a set of preliminary Cora baselines. Q&A follows the 20-minute talk.
Sparse graphs promise lower inference cost
The project asks how to remove edges without losing the useful message-passing structure.
A GNN aggregates information along edges. Fewer edges can reduce computation, but indiscriminate removal can erase useful neighborhood signals.
Can a teacher identify which connections matter?
Measure accuracy and inference cost at matched edge budgets.

Target: 2 minute(s).

Explain the tension: graph sparsity may lower message-passing work, while edge removal can harm node representations. State the outcome measures: test accuracy and inference latency, compared at the same retained-edge budget.
Prior work already prunes edges using learned and structural rules
This project tests teacher-loss scoring plus distillation at matched budgets.
Learns which edges and parameters to remove together. Chen et al. (2021); Unifews (2025) [1, 4].
TEDDY uses degree-based discrimination to trim edges. Seo et al. (2024) [2].
Mixture-of-graphs sparsifiers adapt edge choices by node. Zhang et al. (2025) [3].
Test teacher-loss edge scoring plus distillation at the same edge budget.

Target: 2 minute(s).

Position our method against prior work: joint edge/weight pruning [1,4], TEDDY [2], and node-adaptive sparsification [3]. The proposal tests teacher-loss edge scoring and KD at matched budgets. Feature-similarity pruning is also planned as a baseline.
The student is a smaller GCN with fewer hidden units
Both process the same node features; the student has fewer trainable parameters and uses the retained graph.
EDGE SCORING / KEEP THE TOP-K CONNECTIONS
Same sampled graph nodes; model sizes are compared on the next slide.
Teacher scoring and distillation are proposed; current results are supervised pruning baselines.

Target: 2 minute(s).

The teacher and student are both two-layer GCNs. The illustrative proposal uses 128 hidden units for the teacher and 64 for the student, reducing model parameters. Both use the same node features and output classes; message passing uses full versus retained graph edges. Teacher loss sensitivity ranks edges; the student trains with labels plus soft targets. Compare same-width and smaller KD students to separate distillation gains from capacity effects. Teacher-guided scoring and KD remain proposed; current results are supervised pruning baselines.

Target: 2.5 minute(s).

Make the size distinction concrete: both are two-layer GCNs, but the proposed student uses 64 hidden units against the teacher's 128. This schematic communicates fewer parameters; exact counts depend on input and class dimensions. The student receives retained edges and trains on labels plus softened teacher outputs. The teacher uses the full graph to score edges. These methods are proposed; current results are supervised pruning baselines.

The planned distillation run adds teacher targets after the baseline protocol is fixed.

Target: 2.5 minute(s).

Describe the documented Cora baseline recipe. State that validation accuracy selects checkpoints and test labels are held for final evaluation. The proposal specifies L = (1 - alpha) * CE + alpha * T^2 * KL(pT || pS). α balances label and teacher supervision; T softens the probability targets.
Cora verifies the pipeline; ogbn-arxiv tests scale
The three-seed ogbn-arxiv baseline run is complete; teacher-guided pruning and distillation remain future work.

Target: 2 minute(s).

Cora uses the public Planetoid split. ogbn-arxiv uses the official OGB split by publication year, and its citation graph was made undirected with duplicate connections coalesced. The baseline comparison uses three seeds on an NVIDIA A30. Training time and peak memory are available; inference latency is not yet measured.
These are the proposed teacher-guided pruning and distillation experiments.
Rank connections by sensitivity of the teacher loss.

Test same-width and smaller students; measure accuracy, latency, memory, and scoring cost.
Current results are pruning baselines; the teacher-scoring and distillation stages are next.

Target: 0.5 minute(s).

State the next experiments briefly before the baseline results: score edges from teacher-loss sensitivity, choose edges under a matched budget, train a smaller sparse student with labels and soft targets, and compare it with matched-width controls. Include accuracy, inference latency, memory, and one-time scoring cost. These method stages have not yet been run.
Degree pruning retains more Cora accuracy at the same edge count
Preliminary single-seed results · test accuracy and median forward-pass latency
Random removes about 40.7% of edge entries; degree keeps the same count for a matched-budget comparison.
Latency is noisy in this small run. Treat it as descriptive; do not claim a speedup yet.

Target: 1.5 minute(s).

Read the table and emphasize the matched edge count. Degree pruning is 1.8 percentage points below the full graph, while random pruning is 5.0 points below. Latency is a single run with repeated timings and lacks multi-seed/device-level uncertainty analysis, so avoid a speedup claim.
Degree pruning stays close to full-graph accuracy at 60% of edges
Three seeds on NVIDIA A30 / mean +/- population standard deviation
At 40% edge removal, degree pruning is 0.30 percentage points below full accuracy; random pruning is 1.99 points below.
Degree pruning cuts training-loop time by 35.5% and peak memory by 33.2% versus unpruned.
These are training metrics. ogbn-arxiv inference latency and edge-scoring cost were not reported.

Target: 1.5 minute(s).

All values are three-seed means with population standard deviation. At the same retained edge count, degree-based pruning loses about 0.30 percentage points against the full graph, compared with about 1.99 points for random pruning. The measured time is training-loop time, not inference latency. Peak memory is training peak. Neither edge-scoring overhead nor inference latency was measured in this run.
Preserve label accuracy with fewer edges and a smaller student
Teacher scores edges; the student learns from labels and the teacher's softened predictions.

Target: 1.5 minute(s).

Restate the proposed objective after the baseline results. The teacher ranks edges with the magnitude of its loss gradient with respect to an edge gate. Keep top-K edges, then train a narrower student using the weighted sum of label cross-entropy and temperature-scaled KL divergence to the teacher. This is the planned method, not a result already measured. Accuracy on labels remains the task outcome; distillation adds teacher guidance.
What should the student optimize first?
Accuracy and fidelity can disagree, especially when the teacher is uncertain or wrong.
If they conflict, which should be our primary objective?

Target: 1 minute(s).

Invite the room to discuss whether the smaller student should prioritize ground-truth accuracy or fidelity to the teacher's predictive distribution. Explain that accuracy measures task performance, while fidelity can be measured with KL divergence or prediction agreement. Ask whether fidelity should be a primary goal or a secondary training signal when the teacher itself may be wrong.
